newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - May 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - May 14.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

An annual tax rebate of up to A$450 for every investor is the centrepiece of a Federal Budget which relies on a combination of growth, lower interest payments on debt, the scrapping of the previous Government's L.A.W tax cuts and last year's savings measures, rather than introducing major changes to spending or taxation. Page 1.

In Budget measures which will simplify preservation rules and alleviate the problem of individuals accessing superannuation benefits, spending them and then drawing a pension, people will have to wait longer to access their superannuation, including voluntary contributions. Page A3.

Federal Budget forecasts suggest the new superannuation policies will lift national savings by 1.5 per cent of GDP by the year 2000, rising to 3.6 per cent by 2019-20 - less than the four per cent of GDP by 2020 forecast under the Labor Government's scheme, which focused on compulsory employee
contributions and Government co-contributions using funds from tax cuts. Page A3.

Releasing a discussion paper in the Budget yesterday on a proposal to allow people to access their superannuation to buy their first home, the Federal Government said the scheme, promoted by the Real Estate Institute of Australia, would lower superannuation and increase pension outlays without significantly increasing home ownership. Page A3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

In a Budget that promises a A$1.6 billion underlying Budget surplus in 1998-99, Federal Treasurer Peter Costello has offered a tax rebate of up to A$450 a year on savings and a A$1 billion construction program to create jobs as the centrepiece this year. Costello said under the new policy, every Australian will be eligible for a 15 per cent tax rebate on their savings. Page 1.

In a joint-party-room meeting yesterday that lasted over three hours, Prime Minister John Howard won provisional Coalition party room support for his controversial 10-point Wik native title plan. However, final party approval will not be given to the plan until the legislation is presented to the party room. Page 3.

In comments which come in the wake of the Australian Law Reform Commission's controversial issues paper on the overhaul of Australia's adversarial justice system, Justice Michael Kirby of the High Court launched a strident defence of the national
justice system yesterday and warned against moves to create a career judiciary or dump the adversarial system. Page 3.

The Melbourne Coroners Court was told yesterday 74-year-old Dorothy Joan Meikle, who was terminally ill with motor neurone disease, made a tape recording of her intention to commit suicide so as to absolve her daughter of any involvement in her death. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

In a Federal Budget which was worked around an underlying deficit in 1997-98 of a higher-than-expected A$4 billion, the Government has dismantled the former Keating Government's L.A.W tax cuts, using half of the allocated funds to pay for a new universal savings rebate scheme and pocketing the remainder to deliver its promised surplus next financial year. Page 1.

Under the Federation Fund, announced in the Federal Budget last night to celebrate the Centenary of Federation in 2001, State and Local Governments will be given the chance of competing for a slice of the A$1 billion to be spent on "major
projects of natinal significance". Page 1.

Under a Budget plan to cut more than A$561.4 million from the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme over four years, medicines will cost more, while other common drugs will lose their subsidy altogether. The cut is the biggest single saving in the health budget and will hit the elderly and the chronically ill. Page 38.

In a Budget measure criticised by the Federal Opposition, which says it is really a cut, the Government has pledged A$14.7 million to extend the national Palliative Care Program for another 12 months. The move follows criticism from aged care groups of th Coalition's cuts to palliative care funding in the last Budget. Page 38.
THE AGE

In a cautious Budget released at a time when the Federal Government is suffering in the polls amid growing economic insecurity, Treasurer Peter Costello has unveiled a 15 per cent tax break on all savings. However, the Budget is forecasting little change in the pace of the economy and little reform to appease business criticisms of a "do-nothing" Government. Page 1.

In a move that symbolically tears apart the more expensive plans put forward by the Keating Government in 1995, Federal Treasurer Peter Costello announced last night that six million Australians will be able to claim up to A$450 a year in tax rebates through a new policy that reshapes Australia's superannuation and savings regime. Page 1.

In a change announced in the Budget last night which will impose a new administrative and possible legal burden on business through the provision of a "key features statement" about retirement savings schemes to employees, employers will
have to offer staff the choice of at least five schemes. The move is aimed at breaking the workplace stranglehold of industry and union superannuation funds. Page Budget 1.

Under a Budget plan to be introduced on February 1 to cut the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme by A$560 million over four years, a price subsidy limit will be established for certain "families" of drugs and consumers will have to switch to cheaper drugs unless they want to pay extra. Page Budget 1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
